archetype: Naya Dinosaur typal battlecruiser: a linear critical-mass ramp deck whose entire payoff density is compressed into one commander combat trigger, with a benched 21-card sideboard holding the whole combo package (bracket floor 3, zero contained combos maindeck).

role_assignment.default_role: Quiet ramp player for turns 1-6 — a control POSTURE, not a control deck. Per strategy:whos-the-beatdown the deck's label (aggro battlecruiser) is not its role: until Gishath is castable it cannot race anyone, so it develops mana and manages perceived threat (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection) — while knowing that experienced tables hit exactly the quiet ramp player, so the 'I'm just casting Cultivate' posture gets discounted by anyone tracking mana.
role_assignment.pivot_trigger: The turn Gishath can be cast AND connect: haste means cast-turn combat, so the pivot condition is castable commander + a held protection instant + at least one opponent who cannot profitably block or answer. Per strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window, assume every held answer appears the moment the 8-drop hits the stack, and count open mana before committing — the trigger only pays if combat damage lands. Secondary pivot: a resolved Pantlaza or Descendants' Path engine turn makes the deck the value player and defers the swing.

engines.engine: The core payoff-compression engine: combat damage to a player reveals that many cards, free-rolling every Dinosaur among them onto the battlefield. 34 threat:body entries (deck-facts roles) make the reveal dense. Vigilance/trample/haste means the swing happens the turn he lands. Stack 001 (trigger cascade) has NO checker verdict yet — the trigger's mechanics interactions are candidate, not fact.
engines.evidence: oracle text; deck-facts roles histogram; stack 001 pending

engines.engine: Second, independent engine: once-per-turn discover X = entering Dinosaur's toughness. Unlike Gishath it needs no combat and no 8 mana — it converts every Dinosaur ETB (including Gishath's free-rolls and token creators) into extra spells. It is the engine that keeps working the turn after a wrath.
engines.evidence: oracle text (cards.json); absent from synergy_graph per deck-facts (shortlist artifact, not a fit score)

engines.piece: Urza's Incubator / Belbe's Portal / Monster Manual / Descendants' Path / Huatli, Poet of Unity
engines.engine: The cheat/reducer layer that attacks the 8-mana problem from the cost side: goldfish target 'Cost reducer or cheat-into-play drawn' hits 55.9% by turn 6 (assembled 67.2% overall, mean turn 3.0). Note the deck-facts trap: Unclaimed Territory's mana is spells-only and cannot activate Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual; Secluded Courtyard pays creature-source abilities but Portal/Manual are not creature sources either — both typal lands accelerate the cast plan, not the cheat plan.
engines.evidence: goldfish_metrics.json targets; oracle text; deck-facts notes on restricted mana

engines.piece: Ramp shell (21 lands + 4 ramp:land + 5 rocks + 4 dorks + 3 cost-reduction)
engines.engine: 82% of games see ramp/fixing by turn 6 (goldfish, mean turn 2.2), yet commander mean cast is 7.932 with only 9% by turn 6 — the goldfish does not model cost reducers (stated assumption), so real casts run earlier, but the naked number is the honest picture of the 8-drop problem. 21 lands is far below Duke's ~40% baseline (strategy:deckbuilding.curve); the deck substitutes dorks and rocks, which die to the sweepers it most fears.
engines.evidence: goldfish_metrics.json (mean_cast_turn 7.932, cast_by_turn_6_rate 0.09, ramp target 0.82 by t6); deck-facts roles/curve

engines.piece: Protection suite (Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver, Boros Charm, Akroma's Will, Eerie Interlude)
engines.engine: 49% drawn by turn 6 (goldfish protection target). Five held instants, four of which cover the WHOLE board — this is Cullen's single-use-instant class from strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance, correctly chosen for a deck whose engine hub costs 8 + tax: each removal spell eaten uncovered costs ~2 full turns (recast tax {2} plus the tempo turn). Flawless Maneuver is free with a commander out — it is the swing-turn card.
engines.evidence: oracle text; goldfish target 0.49 by t6 (per pilot brief)

engines.piece: Draw engines (Garruk's Uprising, Curious Altisaur, Bonehoard Dracosaur, Etali, Primal Storm)
engines.engine: Power-4 ETB draw, Dino combat-damage draw, and impulse exile keep the deck rebuilding after a wrath — the cheapest-rebuild criterion of strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math. Curious Altisaur turns every Gishath free-roll swing into cards.

engines.piece: Enrage composition shell (Temple Altisaur + Blasphemous Act maindeck; payoffs benched)
engines.engine: Maindeck holds the asymmetry pieces — Temple Altisaur prevents all but 1 damage to other Dinosaurs; Blasphemous Act costs {1} less per creature — but the enrage PAYOFFS (Polyraptor, Marauding Raptor, Wrathful Raptors, Forerunner, Bellowing Aegisaur, Trapjaw Tyrant, Ranging Raptors...) sit in the 21-card sideboard. Enrage engine hits 49% by t6 per the pilot brief, but its ceiling is bench-gated. This is the pilot's upgrade-path axis.
engines.evidence: oracle text; cards.json is_sideboard flags (21 benched cards); pilot_feedback.md mandate

engines.piece: Top-stack tutors (Congregation at Dawn, Worldly Tutor) + Gishath trigger
engines.engine: Congregation at Dawn puts three creature cards on top in any order — with Gishath's reveal-7 this rigs the free-roll; Worldly Tutor rigs one card for Descendants' Path or Etali. deck-facts shows 9 tutor:narrow slots. This is setup, not a combo: no combo_details record, no stack scenario yet.

How much redirects (13 or 1, per Dinosaur), and what Wrathful itself takes, is unresolved rules work. Wrathful Raptors is benched; Act and Temple are maindeck. — VERDICT: verified one-sided sweep — your Dinosaurs are dealt 1 each under Temple Altisaur (Altisaur takes 13, dies, still redirects 13 via LKI); 16 total redirected to a player; not by itself lethal from 26.

candidate_missing_lines.why_plausible: The trigger itself is oracle text, but the cascade of consequences — Pantlaza's single once-per-turn discover off multiple simultaneous ETBs, draw-trigger ordering, token interactions — is what stack 001 exists to verify. Until checker passes, no claim about the trigger's downstream sequencing is fact. — VERDICT: verified (5 bodies, 3 draws, discover X=6; trigger-ordering matters — discover before the Regisaur token).

matchup_frames.vs_sweeper_control: The deck's worst frame: a board built by one Gishath trigger is one sweeper from zero, and 'deploy in waves' (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) is structurally unavailable — the trigger IS the wave. So buy resilience, not restraint: the swing should happen only with a board-wide protection instant held (Flawless Maneuver is free with the commander out), timed into the control player's tapped-out turn (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). After a wrath, Pantlaza + draw engines are the cheapest-rebuild package; redeploy worst-first and keep Gishath recastable. Note also strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance: every uncovered removal spell on Gishath costs {2} more plus a tempo turn — two answered casts roughly ends the game plan.
matchup_frames.vs_stax: Cost taxes hit an 8-drop harder than anyone else at the table; the cheat layer (Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, Descendants' Path, Incubator) is the tax-resistant route, so per strategy:critical-mass the fight is over enablers, not payoffs — protect and sequence the cheat pieces first, and mulligan toward them (strategy:mulligans.engine-hands: payoffs without the enabler are blanks). Watch the deck-facts trap: Unclaimed Territory cannot activate Portal or Manual. Removal budget (6 spot, per roles) goes to the stax piece that turns off the cheat layer specifically, not the scariest permanent (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy).
matchup_frames.vs_aggro: The deck owns the long game — an 8/7-ish commander that refills the board on connect is inevitability by Duke's definition (strategy:whos-the-beatdown.metagame-clock) — so against faster aggro it takes the control role: big vigilant blockers, Blasphemous Act as a catch-up sweeper (cheap against their wide board), spot removal on the one threat that actually races (strategy:threat-assessment). Turn the corner immediately on stabilizing (strategy:combat-math.racing): every passive turn after stabilization is a free draw step for them, and Gishath's haste makes the corner-turn violent.
matchup_frames.vs_combo: The bad seat. The maindeck has zero contained combos and a thin interaction suite (6 spot removal, 2 sweepers, 4 damage-based per deck-facts roles) with no counterspells in Naya; the clock is real but starts around turn 6-8. Per strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy the held-answers-rot clause governs: against combo the last profitable moment is now — spend removal on enablers (draw engines, tutors, the combo hub) rather than banking it, and race honestly the rest of the way. Per strategy:whos-the-beatdown, this matchup forces the beatdown role regardless of posture: playing control here concedes the only axis available.

distribution_notes: Curve mode is 3 (17 entries) over 65 nonland spells with 21 lands + 13 mana producers + 3 reducers — a mana-heavy bottom (roughly 40% of the deck makes or reduces mana) supporting a 34-body typal top. Goldfish: ramp/fixing 82% by t6 (mean turn 2.2) but land-drop hit rate falls to 52% by t6 and mean available mana is only 5.5 at t6 — the deck ramps early then relies on rocks/dorks, exactly the profile a mid-game sweeper punishes twice (board AND mana). Commander mean cast 7.932, median 8, 9% by t6, 54.6% of goldfish games never cast him by turn 10 — though the simulator explicitly does not model the cost reducers or cheat pieces (56% drawn by t6), so treat 7.93 as the ceiling of the problem, not the expectation. Pip picture is comfortable: G 53 total pips dominates (38 cards), source targets 36/36/36 vs land sources G11/R12/W9 — the colour weight rides on the 13 nonland producers. Role coverage 93%; the six no-role cards (Descendants' Path, Eerie Interlude, Hunter's Insight, Overwhelming Stampede, Rishkar's Expertise, Triumphant Chomp) are real functions the taxonomy lacks patterns for, not dead slots.
overall_assessment: This is a linear critical-mass deck (strategy:critical-mass) wearing battlecruiser clothes: every card either accelerates toward, cheapens, protects, or cashes in one event — Gishath connecting. The game it plays is a seven-turn setup into a single pivot (strategy:pivot-point): turns 1-6 in a deflection posture as the quiet ramp player (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection), knowing that posture is discounted by good tables, then one haste swing that must be timed like a combo turn (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window) — protection held, table's mana counted, sweeper assumed (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Its two structural tensions are honest weaknesses: the payoff arrives as one wrath-sized package on a commander whose recast tax is ruinous (strategy:multiplayer.commander-insurance), and its enrage sub-engine wants damage dealt to its own creatures that a table under no obligation to attack a Temple Altisaur board will not volunteer — the deck must bring its own damage (Blasphemous Act, Itzquinth, Forerunner-from-bench), which is precisely where the sideboard's combo package lives. Pantlaza and the draw engines are what elevate it from all-in to resilient: they are the rebuild after the wrath and the engine that does not need combat. The pilot's aggressive upgrade-path mandate has a clear shape: every verified bench line (002/003/004 pending) converts the enrage tension from a liability into the win condition — but not one of those lines is fact until its checker verdict lands.
